I will never forget the look of hope on his face that day. He had spent his life tortured by the thought that the world had looked away from the Jewish people as the Nazis filled the gas chambers and crematoria with our brothers and sisters, aunts and uncles, children. Finally, he felt seen, and he had a message to share. As he put it in his acceptance speech, “We must always take sides. Neutrality helps the oppressor, never the victim.” My father was honored because he had turned the memory of genocide into a moral duty to the living. articles.author: Prashant Rao
articles.summary: Navi Pillay, a South African jurist who was the UN’s longest-serving human rights chief, was awarded the Nobel Peace Prize . Pillay was a pioneer long before taking on major international roles: She was the first non-white woman to serve as a judge in South Africa’s High Court. But it has been her time on the global stage — and her particular focus on genocide — that has won her most plaudits, beginning with the tribunal over ethnic cleansing in Rwanda. The focus has made her a controversial figure, however, particularly in countries she argues have carried out genocide; she told The Guardian last year that she saw echoes of the Rwandan killings in Israel’s war in Gaza , which Israel angrily dismissed. — Prashant Rao

articles.summary: Before the mid-19th century, executions in America were presumptively public. Most prisoners were hanged on a gallows, following an hours-long affair that began with the condemned person’s exit from jail accompanied by ministers, the sheriff and his deputies, and sometimes a military escort. Spectators joined the humiliating procession, gathering by the thousands to watch the noose lowered over the prisoner’s neck.
